prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.

text:
Suppose two people, call them Alice and Bob, want to share a secret number that they can then use as the key to scramble their messages, but the only way they can talk is a line that anyone may tap, so that every word either of them says is heard by an eavesdropper, Eve, as well as by the person it was meant for. Before the 1970s it seemed obvious that this could not be done, because a shared secret had always been something carried in person, in a codebook or on a slip of paper, and if two people had never met there was nothing for them to carry. The surprise of public-key cryptography is that Alice and Bob can build a secret together out of things that are all spoken aloud, provided they use a kind of arithmetic in which some operations are easy to do and almost impossible to undo.

The idea is easiest to see with paint before any numbers appear. Imagine that Alice and Bob publicly agree on a shared colour, say yellow, which Eve also knows. Each of them privately picks a secret colour of their own, Alice a particular red and Bob a particular blue, and mixes it with the yellow, so that Alice ends up with an orange-ish mixture and Bob with a greenish one. They send these mixtures to each other across the open line, and Eve can see both mixtures and the yellow they started from. Now Alice adds her secret red to the mixture she received from Bob, and Bob adds his secret blue to the mixture he received from Alice, and since each batch now contains yellow plus red plus blue, both end up with exactly the same final colour. Eve cannot reproduce it, because to do so she would need to separate a mixture back into its ingredients, and unmixing paint is the hard direction while mixing is the easy one. Real systems need a mathematical version of this one-way mixing, and school arithmetic provides one if we change how we count.

Think of a clock, where after twelve comes one again and nine hours after four o'clock is one o'clock, because thirteen wraps round to one. Mathematicians call this counting by remainders, or modular arithmetic, and it works with any size of clock, not only twelve, so we can say that something is "the remainder after dividing by 23" and mean the position you land on a 23-hour clock face after going round as many times as necessary. On such a clock, multiplication behaves in a way that looks scrambled: if you start with 5 and keep multiplying by 5, taking the remainder on the 23-hour clock each time, you get 5, then 2 (since 25 is one full turn plus 2), then 10, then 4, then 20, then 8, then 17, and so on, bouncing around the face with no visible pattern. Raising a number to a power, which means multiplying it by itself many times, therefore leaves you somewhere that looks random, and although there is a quick method for computing such a position even when the power is enormous, nobody has found a quick method for going backwards, that is, for looking at the final position and working out how many multiplications it took. That one-way behaviour is the paint mixing of the mathematical version.

Here is the agreement carried out with small numbers. Alice and Bob announce publicly that they will use the 23-hour clock and the starting number 5. Alice secretly chooses 6 and computes what 5 becomes after multiplying by itself six times on that clock, which is 15625, and since 23 goes into that 679 times with 8 left over, her result is 8. Bob secretly chooses 15 and does the same with fifteen multiplications, which, if he is careful to take remainders as he goes, gives him 19. Alice sends 8 and Bob sends 19, in the open, where Eve hears both. Alice now takes Bob's 19 and multiplies it by itself six times, her own secret number, which lands on 2, and Bob takes Alice's 8 and multiplies it by itself fifteen times, his secret number, which also lands on 2. They have agreed on the number 2 without ever saying it, and the reason they agree is that both have in effect multiplied 5 by itself six times fifteen times, which is ninety, in two different orders, and the order of a pile of multiplications does not change the result.

Eve's position is that she knows the clock size 23, the starting number 5, and the two announced results 8 and 19, but she knows neither 6 nor 15, and she needs one of them to reach the answer. With a clock as small as 23 she could simply try every possibility, noticing that 5 multiplied by itself six times gives 8, and from there compute what Alice computed, so this toy example offers no real protection. Its only purpose is to show the shape of the method, and the protection comes entirely from scaling up. In real use the clock has hundreds of digits, which is far more positions than there are atoms in the observable universe, and the secret numbers are similarly huge, so that trying every possibility would take longer than the age of the universe on every computer ever built, while the honest parties, using the quick method for powers, finish in a fraction of a second. The security rests on this gap between the easy forward direction and the infeasible backward one, and it is a bet that nobody will find a shortcut, a bet that has survived decades of serious effort by mathematicians who would love to win it, though it is a bet and not a proof.

The name public-key cryptography comes from a slightly different but closely related arrangement, in which each person owns a pair of numbers, one made public and one kept secret, built so that anything locked with the public one can be unlocked only with the secret one. You can picture a padlock that Bob manufactures and hands out freely to anyone, which snaps shut without a key, while only Bob holds the key that opens it, so that Alice, a stranger, can lock a message in his padlock and send it, and not even she can open it again. The agreement described above is the same principle seen from the side of two people building a shared secret, and in practice the two ideas are combined, because the heavy lifting of scrambling a long message is done by an ordinary fast method that needs a single shared key, and public-key mathematics is used only to get that key safely from one side to the other at the start of the conversation. This is what happens, invisibly, when your browser shows a padlock and connects to a bank, a shop or a messaging service you have never dealt with before.

There is one weakness that the mathematics alone does not fix, which is that Alice does not know for certain that the number she receives really came from Bob. If Eve can do more than listen, and can sit in the middle of the line, she can run one agreement with Alice and another with Bob, pass messages between them, and read everything in between while each believes they are talking privately to the other. Defending against this requires a way for Bob to prove who he is, which is done with the same kind of paired numbers used in reverse, so that Bob signs something with his secret number in a way that anyone can check with his public one, and with trusted organisations vouching that a given public number really belongs to a given name. The secret agreement over an open line is therefore only half the story, but it is the surprising half, the part that overturned the assumption that secrecy needs a prior meeting, and it rests on nothing more exotic than the fact that on a clock face it is easy to wind forward and hard to wind back.
